dataIdInfo.idPurp: This dataset was developed to systematically identify and demarcate landslide-affected areas caused by Cyclone Ditwah – 2025 using satellite remote sensing data. The primary objective is to support disaster management, damage assessment, and post-disaster response planning by providing reliable spatial information on landslide extents.

dataIdInfo.idAbs:
The Arthur C. Clarke Institute for Modern Technologies is the national mandated institute for space science activities in Sri Lanka. Following the prolonged rainfall associated with the Ditwah cyclone during November–December 2025, we mapped and demarcated more than 4,000 mass movements and widespread slope failures across the country. Using Sentinel-2 satellite imagery and advanced Remote Sensing and GIS techniques, a national landslide boundary demarcation dataset was developed as a timely and important contribution to disaster risk reduction and sustainable land management in Sri Lanka. Sentinel-2 provides freely available multispectral data at 10–20 m spatial resolution with frequent revisit times, making it well suited for mapping landslide extents over large and difficult-to-access areas.

Previous landslide demarcations are essential for understanding and predicting future landslide activity. As widely recognized, the best predictor of future landslides is the location of past landslides. Areas that have failed in the past usually contain weak slope conditions and therefore remain vulnerable to future failures. The developed dataset enables authorities to rapidly identify affected zones and estimate the spatial extent of damage, supporting decision-making for road clearance, restoration of utilities, and relocation planning by clearly indicating unstable or failed slopes. In addition, past landslide maps serve as reliable reference data for training and validating landslide prediction models. In process-based models such as RAMMS, previous landslide boundaries help define realistic release areas and estimate landslide volumes, while comparisons between simulated results and observed landslides support model validation and reduce uncertainty.
